claims.text: The structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature is governed by formation of a stable surface oxide layer.
A stable surface oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
A stable surface oxide layer acts as a barrier to degradation.
Heating a clean high-entropy nanoalloy above 500°C in an inert atmosphere will produce a stable oxide layer.
The oxide layer reduces oxidation rates by acting as a diffusion barrier.
The oxide layer reduces degradation rates by acting as a diffusion barrier.
A nanoalloy with a stable oxide layer will exhibit greater high-temperature stability than an otherwise comparable nanoalloy without such a layer or with a non-stable oxide layer.
A nanoalloy with a stable oxide layer will exhibit less high-temperature degradation than the stated baseline.
The prediction is intended to apply from 500°C to 1000°C in inert atmospheres such as argon or nitrogen.
The composition and structure of the stable oxide layer may depend on the specific high-entropy nanoalloy composition.

contradictions.description: The initial surface is specified as clean and heating occurs in an inert atmosphere, yet stable oxide-layer formation is posited without specifying an oxygen source, prior oxide preparation, or controlled oxidizing exposure.
